questions.stem: Which structure marks the boundary between the upper and lower airway?

options.rationale: The epiglottis is part of the upper airway; it guards the entrance to the larynx but is not the dividing line.
Correct. The upper airway ends at the larynx; the lower airway begins with the trachea just below it.
The carina is well into the lower airway, where the trachea splits into the two mainstem bronchi.
The oropharynx is the middle section of the pharynx, entirely within the upper airway.

questions.stem: The function of the epiglottis is to:

options.rationale: Sound is produced by the vocal cords within the larynx, not the epiglottis.

options.text: Cover the opening of the trachea during swallowing
options.rationale: Correct. The leaf-shaped epiglottis folds over the glottic opening so food and liquid go to the esophagus rather than the lungs.
Warming and humidifying happen in the nasal passages.
Gas exchange occurs only in the alveoli.

questions.stem: The most common cause of airway obstruction in an unresponsive patient lying supine is:

options.rationale: Foreign bodies cause obstruction, but far less often than the tongue in an unresponsive patient.
Correct. Loss of muscle tone lets the tongue fall back against the posterior pharynx. Positioning maneuvers correct this.
Epiglottitis is a real but uncommon cause, mostly in specific infections.
The adult trachea is supported by cartilage rings and does not collapse under normal conditions.

questions.stem: Gas exchange between the air and the blood takes place in the:

options.rationale: The bronchi are conducting airways; no gas exchange occurs there.
The trachea only conducts air to and from the lungs.
Correct. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the thin alveolar-capillary membrane.
The larynx houses the vocal cords and marks the top of the lower airway; it does not exchange gas.

questions.stem: When positioning an infant's airway, the EMT places padding under the shoulders because:

options.text: Infants have a proportionally large occiput that flexes the neck when supine
options.rationale: Correct. The large back of the head tips the chin toward the chest, folding the airway; padding restores a neutral position.

options.text: Infants have weak neck muscles that need support
options.rationale: Muscle strength is not the reason; skull proportion is.

options.text: It elevates the chest to improve breathing
options.rationale: The padding goes under the shoulders to level the head, not to raise the chest.

options.text: It prevents the tongue from falling forward
options.rationale: The tongue falls backward, not forward, and the padding addresses head position, not the tongue directly.

questions.stem: The narrowest point of a young child's airway is the:

options.rationale: The vocal cords (glottic opening) are the narrowest point in an adult, not a young child.
Correct. In young children the cricoid cartilage is the narrowest point, giving the airway a funnel shape.
The nasal passages are small but are not the narrowest point of the airway.
The carina is a branch point in the lower airway, not the narrowest part.

questions.stem: Hyperextending a small child's neck during a head-tilt/chin-lift may:

options.text: Improve airflow by straightening the airway
options.rationale: In adults, extension helps. In small children the opposite can occur.

options.text: Kink the soft trachea and obstruct the airway
options.rationale: Correct. The pediatric trachea has little cartilage support; overextension can collapse it. Use only slight extension in children and a neutral position in infants.

options.text: Have no effect on the airway
options.rationale: Head position has a major effect on the pediatric airway.

options.text: Cause the epiglottis to seal the trachea
options.rationale: The epiglottis does not close in response to head extension.

questions.stem: Compared with adults, children who stop breathing become hypoxic more quickly because they:

options.rationale: Backwards. Children have a faster metabolic rate.

options.text: Have a higher metabolic rate and less oxygen reserve
options.rationale: Correct. Children consume oxygen faster and have less stored in the lungs, so desaturation is rapid.

options.text: Have larger lungs relative to body size
options.rationale: Pediatric lung volume relative to oxygen demand is smaller, not larger.
Infants rely heavily on the diaphragm; that is not the reason for rapid hypoxia.

questions.stem: The mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs is called:

options.rationale: Respiration is gas exchange, not air movement.
Correct. Ventilation is the physical movement of air; it says nothing about whether gas exchange is occurring.
Oxygenation is oxygen loading onto hemoglobin and delivery to tissues.
Perfusion is blood flow through tissues.

questions.stem: A patient pulled from a house fire is breathing 16 times a minute with full chest rise but is confused and has a headache. Which process is most likely failing?

options.rationale: Air is moving normally, so ventilation is intact.
Correct. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin, so oxygen cannot load and reach tissues even though air movement is normal.

options.text: Both ventilation and respiration have stopped
options.rationale: Air is moving and gas is still crossing the alveoli; the failure is at the hemoglobin.

options.text: Nothing; the patient is breathing normally
options.rationale: A confused fire victim with a headache is hypoxic until proven otherwise, regardless of normal chest rise.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm CO mechanism wording in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: An adult breathes 12 times per minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. What is the minute volume?

options.rationale: That is one breath's tidal volume, not the total per minute.
This is alveolar ventilation after subtracting 150 mL dead space, which the question did not ask for.
Correct. Minute volume = tidal volume × rate = 500 × 12 = 6,000 mL.
This doubles the tidal volume; check the multiplication.

questions.stem: Why is rapid, shallow breathing less effective than the rate alone suggests?

options.text: A larger share of each breath is wasted on dead space that never reaches the alveoli
options.rationale: Correct. About 150 mL of every breath fills the conducting airways; with a 200 mL breath, only 50 mL reaches the alveoli.

options.text: Fast breathing lowers the oxygen concentration of inhaled air
options.rationale: Inhaled air is 21% oxygen regardless of rate.

options.text: The alveoli close at high respiratory rates
options.rationale: Alveoli do not close because of rate.

options.text: The diaphragm cannot contract at rates above 20
options.rationale: The diaphragm functions at much higher rates; the issue is volume, not muscle capacity.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm dead space explanation in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: The normal respiratory rate for an adult at rest is:

options.rationale: Below the normal adult range; a rate of 8 is bradypnea.
Correct. This is the standard adult range.
This is the range for a child.
This is the range for an infant.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old is breathing 40 times per minute, alert, with even chest rise and no retractions. This rate is:

options.rationale: Ventilation is for inadequate breathing. This infant is alert with easy, even breathing.
Correct. Infants breathe about 25 to 50 times per minute; 40 with no signs of effort is normal.
40 is within, not below, the infant range.

options.text: Normal only if the infant is crying
options.rationale: The rate is normal at rest; crying would push it higher.

questions.stem: The best technique for counting a patient's respiratory rate is to:

options.text: Tell the patient you are counting so they breathe normally
options.rationale: Awareness changes the rate. Never announce that you are counting.

options.text: Watch the chest for 30 seconds and double the count while appearing to take a pulse
options.rationale: Correct. This gives an accurate rate without the patient consciously altering their breathing.

options.text: Count for 5 seconds and multiply by 12
options.rationale: Too short an interval to be accurate, especially with irregular breathing.

options.text: Ask the patient how fast they are breathing
options.rationale: Patients cannot reliably report their own rate.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man is breathing 8 times per minute with shallow chest rise and is difficult to arouse. The most appropriate action is to:

options.text: Apply a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
options.rationale: A passive mask cannot fix a rate and depth that are too low. This patient is not ventilating adequately.

options.text: Begin ventilations with a bag-valve-mask and supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Correct. Inadequate rate, inadequate depth, and altered mental status: this patient needs positive-pressure ventilation now.

options.text: Place a nasal cannula at 4 L/min and reassess
options.rationale: Far too little support for a patient in respiratory failure.

options.text: Place the patient in the recovery position and monitor
options.rationale: Positioning does not correct inadequate ventilation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a LATE sign of inadequate breathing?

options.rationale: Nasal flaring is an early sign of increased work of breathing.
Tripoding is an early compensatory posture.
Correct. Blue or gray skin means hypoxia is already severe; do not wait for it before acting.
Short phrases signal distress but appear well before cyanosis.

questions.stem: A patient is making slow, irregular gasping breaths about four times a minute. The EMT should treat this patient as:

options.rationale: Agonal gasps are not effective breathing.
Correct. Agonal gasps come from a failing brainstem and move no useful air. Manage as apnea.
Four gasps a minute is the opposite of hyperventilation.
Agonal respirations are a sign of impending or actual cardiac arrest, not a seizure.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with asthma is sitting upright, leaning forward on her hands, and can say only two or three words before pausing to breathe. Her rate is 30 and her SpO2 is 88%. These findings indicate:

options.text: Adequate breathing with mild hypoxia; nasal cannula
options.rationale: Tripod position, two-word dyspnea, and a rate of 30 are signs of significant distress, not mild hypoxia.

options.text: Inadequate breathing with significant distress; high-concentration oxygen now and prepare to assist ventilations
options.rationale: Correct. She is still moving air, so start with a non-rebreather and her inhaler per protocol, but the effort signs mean she may tire and need BVM assistance. Reassess constantly.

options.text: Normal breathing for an asthma patient
options.rationale: There is no 'normal' that includes tripoding and two-word dyspnea.
Hypoxia at 88% with a known asthma history is not hyperventilation syndrome.

questions.stem: In an unresponsive patient, which structure is most likely to be obstructing the airway?

options.rationale: Correct. In an unresponsive patient the tongue is the structure most likely to be against the back of the throat.
Teeth can be a foreign-body concern but are not the usual cause of obstruction in an unresponsive patient.
The diaphragm is a muscle of ventilation, not a structure that obstructs the upper airway.
Tracheal cartilage holds the airway open rather than blocking it.

options.text: There is no reason to suspect a spinal injury
options.rationale: Correct. It is the first choice when the mechanism does not raise spinal concern.

options.text: The mechanism strongly suggests a spinal injury
options.rationale: That is the situation the other maneuver exists for.

options.text: The patient is awake and talking
options.rationale: A patient who is talking is maintaining their own airway.

options.text: The patient is already breathing normally
options.rationale: A patient breathing normally on their own does not need the maneuver.

options.text: Pick the maneuver that matches the mechanism of injury
options.rationale: Correct. The pairing is a mechanism question wearing an airway question's clothes.

options.text: Can name the anatomy of the upper airway
options.rationale: Naming anatomy is tested elsewhere, not by this pairing.
Flow rates belong to the oxygen delivery lesson.

options.text: Can size an airway adjunct correctly
options.rationale: Adjunct sizing is a separate skill with its own questions.

options.text: The patient is a child rather than an adult

questions.stem: Choosing between head-tilt/chin-lift and jaw-thrust is driven entirely by:

Neither maneuver requires equipment.

questions.stem: At what cylinder pressure should an EMT replace an oxygen cylinder?

options.rationale: Running a cylinder empty allows moisture and contaminants in and gives unreliable flow near the end. Never plan to run one dry.
Correct. 200 psi is the safe residual pressure. At that reading the cylinder is swapped or refilled.
Plenty of usable oxygen remains at 500 psi. Swapping this early wastes supply and time.
A cylinder at 1,000 psi is roughly half full and has significant usable volume.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm safe residual pressure in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: A D cylinder reads 1,700 psi. The patient is on a non-rebreather at 15 L/min. Approximately how long will the cylinder last?

options.rationale: This is what you get if you forget the constant and just divide. The constant accounts for cylinder volume.
This results from forgetting to subtract the 200 psi safe residual: 1,700 × 0.16 ÷ 15 = 18.1. The residual is not usable.
This uses the E cylinder constant (0.28) on a D cylinder. Match the constant to the cylinder size.

questions.stem: Which action is a safety violation when handling an oxygen cylinder?

options.text: Opening the cylinder valve slowly while standing to the side of the regulator
options.rationale: This is correct practice. Slow opening and staying out of line with the regulator protects you if a fitting fails.

options.text: Applying a small amount of grease to a stiff regulator fitting
options.rationale: Correct. Petroleum products can ignite violently in the presence of pressurized oxygen. Never use oil or grease on oxygen equipment.

options.text: Securing the cylinder in a bracket before transport
options.rationale: Securing the cylinder is required. An unsecured cylinder can become a projectile if the valve breaks.

options.text: Checking the hydrostatic test date stamped on the cylinder
options.rationale: Checking the test date is part of proper equipment inspection.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm safety rules list in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: What is the function of the regulator on an oxygen cylinder?

options.text: It increases the pressure so oxygen can be delivered through long tubing
options.rationale: Pressure needs to go down, not up. Cylinder pressure is far too high to deliver to a patient.

options.text: It reduces the high cylinder pressure to a safe working pressure
options.rationale: Correct. The regulator drops roughly 2,000 psi to a safe working pressure; the attached flowmeter then sets liters per minute.

options.text: It humidifies the oxygen before it reaches the patient
options.rationale: Humidification is done by a separate humidifier bottle, not the regulator.

options.text: It filters carbon dioxide out of the oxygen supply
options.rationale: Medical oxygen cylinders contain oxygen only; no CO2 filtering is involved.

questions.stem: A nasal cannula should be set to a flow rate of:

options.rationale: Correct. This is the working range for a cannula, delivering roughly 24% to 44% oxygen.
Flow above 6 L/min dries the nasal passages without meaningfully raising the concentration. This range is closer to a partial rebreather.
This is the non-rebreather range. A cannula at this flow is uncomfortable and ineffective.
No standard EMT device runs at this flow. It is beyond the range of the cannula and the NRB.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm cannula flow range in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: Which patient is the best candidate for a nasal cannula?

options.text: A 70-year-old who is breathing 8 times per minute with shallow chest rise
options.rationale: This patient is breathing inadequately and needs ventilation with a BVM, not a passive oxygen device.

options.text: A 55-year-old with chest pain, speaking in full sentences, SpO2 91%
options.rationale: Correct. Breathing adequately, mildly hypoxic, and needs only a modest oxygen boost. Titrate toward 94% to 99%.

options.text: A 30-year-old asthmatic in obvious distress with SpO2 84%
options.rationale: Severe hypoxia with distress calls for a non-rebreather. A cannula cannot deliver enough oxygen.

options.text: A 40-year-old with a broken nose and both nostrils packed with blood
options.rationale: Nasal obstruction defeats the cannula; the oxygen never reaches the airway. Use a mask.

questions.stem: The approximate oxygen concentration delivered by a nasal cannula is:

options.rationale: 21% is room air. A cannula adds oxygen on top of that.
Correct. Across its 1 to 6 L/min range a cannula delivers roughly 24% to 44%.
This is closer to a partial rebreather's range, not a cannula.
That is the non-rebreather. A cannula cannot approach this concentration.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm cannula concentration range in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: Your patient on a nasal cannula at 6 L/min still has an SpO2 of 90%. The best next step is to:

options.rationale: More flow through a cannula dries the nose without adding meaningful concentration. The device is at its ceiling.

options.text: Switch to a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
options.rationale: Correct. When a cannula cannot get the patient into the target range, change the device to one that delivers more, and reassess breathing adequacy.

options.text: Leave the cannula in place and reassess in 15 minutes
options.rationale: A sat below the target with a device already maxed out is a reason to act now, not wait.
A hypoxic patient needs more oxygen, not less.

questions.stem: A non-rebreather mask set at 15 L/min delivers an oxygen concentration of approximately:

options.rationale: This is the top of the nasal cannula range.
This is roughly the top of a partial rebreather's range, which lacks the NRB's one-way valve.
Correct. With a properly inflated reservoir and 10 to 15 L/min, an NRB delivers up to about 90%.
The mask is not perfectly sealed and always entrains a little room air, so it does not reach 100%.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm NRB delivered concentration in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: Before placing a non-rebreather mask on a patient, the EMT must:

options.rationale: 6 L/min is too low for an NRB; the reservoir will collapse and concentration will fall.
Correct. Occlude the valve so the bag fills completely, so the patient's first breath draws high-concentration oxygen.

options.text: Remove the one-way valves so the patient can exhale easily
options.rationale: The valves are what make it a non-rebreather. Removing them lets exhaled air back into the reservoir and drops the concentration.

options.text: Confirm the patient is not breathing
options.rationale: Backwards. The NRB requires a patient who is breathing adequately. A non-breathing patient needs a BVM.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm NRB application steps in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: You arrive to find a 60-year-old man who is unresponsive, breathing 6 times per minute with shallow, irregular respirations, and cyanotic around the lips. Which oxygen delivery method is most appropriate?

options.rationale: A cannula cannot correct inadequate breathing and delivers too little oxygen for this patient.
The NRB depends on the patient breathing adequately on his own. At 6 shallow breaths per minute he is not, so the mask is oxygen sitting on a face.
Correct. Inadequate rate and depth require positive-pressure ventilation. The BVM both ventilates and delivers high-concentration oxygen.
A Venturi mask delivers a controlled low concentration and, like any passive mask, does not help a patient who is not breathing adequately.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm NRB vs BVM decision criteria in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: While your patient is on a non-rebreather, you notice the reservoir bag collapsing almost completely with each breath. You should:

options.rationale: Correct. A collapsing reservoir means the flow is not keeping up with the patient's demand. Turn it up until the bag stays at least two-thirds full.

options.text: Loosen the mask strap to let in more room air
options.rationale: Letting in room air lowers the oxygen concentration. That is the opposite of the goal.
A patient drawing this hard needs more oxygen, not a lower-concentration device.
The reservoir is what makes the NRB work. Without it the mask becomes a simple face mask with much lower concentration.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm reservoir collapse guidance in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: Which oxygen delivery device provides the most precise, controlled oxygen concentration?

options.rationale: The NRB delivers high concentration but not a precise, adjustable percentage.
Correct. Color-coded adapters entrain a fixed ratio of room air to deliver a specific concentration, roughly 24% to 50%.
The partial rebreather's concentration varies with the patient's breathing and is not precisely controlled.
Cannula concentration varies widely with the patient's breathing pattern and is not precise.

questions.stem: The main difference between a partial rebreather mask and a non-rebreather mask is that the partial rebreather:

options.rationale: Bag size is similar. The difference is in the valves, not the bag.

options.text: Lacks the one-way valve between the mask and the reservoir, so some exhaled air is rebreathed
options.rationale: Correct. Without that valve, part of each exhaled breath returns to the bag, lowering the delivered concentration.
It delivers a lower concentration, roughly 40% to 60%, because of the rebreathing.

options.text: Is used for patients who are not breathing
options.rationale: Like all passive masks, it requires adequate spontaneous breathing.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm partial rebreather description in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: Humidified oxygen is most appropriate for:

options.text: A 10-minute transport of an adult with chest pain
options.rationale: Short transports do not need humidification; dry oxygen for a few minutes causes no meaningful harm.

options.text: A 90-minute interfacility transfer of a pediatric patient on continuous oxygen
options.rationale: Correct. Prolonged administration and pediatric patients are the classic indications, because dry oxygen irritates the airway over time.

options.text: A patient in cardiac arrest receiving BVM ventilation
options.rationale: Humidification is not a priority during resuscitation; ventilation and compressions are.
Routine humidification is unnecessary for typical short EMS calls.

questions.stem: You are treating a patient rescued from a house fire. She is confused with a headache, but her pulse oximeter reads 99%. The most likely explanation is:

options.text: She is adequately oxygenated and does not need supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: A confused, symptomatic fire victim with a perfect reading should raise suspicion, not reassurance.

options.text: Carbon monoxide is bound to her hemoglobin and the oximeter cannot distinguish it from oxygen
options.rationale: Correct. Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as saturated hemoglobin, giving a falsely high value. Treat with high-flow oxygen regardless of the number.

options.text: The probe is on too tightly
options.rationale: A tight probe may reduce signal quality but does not produce a falsely high reading in this pattern.
A dirty sensor typically gives no reading or a poor signal, not a confidently high one.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm CO and pulse oximetry statement in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to cause an inaccurate pulse oximetry reading?

options.rationale: Position does not affect the reading.

options.text: The patient has cold hands and poor circulation
options.rationale: Correct. The device needs a strong pulsatile signal; cold, poorly perfused fingers give weak or false readings.
Food intake has no effect on oximetry.

options.text: The patient is on a nasal cannula
options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen changes the true saturation but does not make the reading inaccurate.

questions.stem: A patient with obvious labored breathing and accessory muscle use has a pulse oximeter reading of 97%. The EMT should:

options.text: Withhold oxygen because the saturation is normal
options.rationale: The patient's presentation outranks the number. Visible distress is treated.

options.text: Treat the patient's distress and continue to assess, regardless of the reading
options.rationale: Correct. SpO2 reflects oxygenation only; a patient can be working hard and heading toward failure with a normal number. Treat what you see.

options.text: Assume the oximeter is broken and replace it
options.rationale: The reading may be accurate. The lesson is that a normal SpO2 does not rule out inadequate ventilation, not that the device is faulty.

options.text: Document the reading and take no further action
options.rationale: A patient in labored breathing always requires intervention and reassessment.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm 'treat the patient not the monitor' guidance in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: Pulse oximetry measures:

options.text: The amount of carbon dioxide in exhaled breath
options.rationale: That is capnography, a separate device.

options.text: The percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen
options.rationale: Correct. SpO2 is the percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen (or, unfortunately, carbon monoxide).
Respiratory rate is counted by observation; some monitors estimate it, but that is not what pulse oximetry measures.

options.text: The partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
options.rationale: PaO2 requires an arterial blood gas. SpO2 is an estimate of saturation, not partial pressure.

questions.stem: For most acutely ill patients, supplemental oxygen should be titrated to maintain an SpO2 of:

options.rationale: This is below the accepted target and represents hypoxia in most patients.
This is the lower target used for some CO2-retaining COPD patients, not the general population.
Correct. This is the current target for most patients; give oxygen when below it and avoid pushing beyond it.
Routinely driving saturation to 100% is no longer recommended and may be harmful in some conditions.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm target range in AAOS 12e and current AHA guidance.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with a history of severe COPD is cyanotic, confused, and breathing 30 times per minute with an SpO2 of 78%. Your partner hesitates to give oxygen because 'COPD patients can stop breathing with too much oxygen.' The correct action is to:

options.rationale: Withholding oxygen from a severely hypoxic, cyanotic patient is never correct. Hypoxia kills far faster than hypercapnia.

options.text: Give high-concentration oxygen now and monitor breathing and mental status closely, titrating per protocol
options.rationale: Correct. A COPD patient in true distress gets oxygen. The hypoxic-drive concern means you watch and titrate, not that you withhold.

options.text: Apply a nasal cannula at 1 L/min and reassess in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Far too little oxygen for a patient this hypoxic, and too long a wait.

options.text: Have the patient breathe into a paper bag
options.rationale: This has no role here and would worsen hypoxia.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm COPD oxygen guidance in AAOS 12e.

questions.stem: A patient with chest pain suggestive of a heart attack is alert, breathing comfortably, and has an SpO2 of 97%. Regarding oxygen, the EMT should:

options.text: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 L/min because all cardiac patients receive high-flow oxygen
options.rationale: This was old practice. Routine high-flow oxygen for non-hypoxic cardiac patients is no longer recommended.

options.text: Withhold supplemental oxygen unless the SpO2 falls below 94% or distress develops, per protocol
options.rationale: Correct. The patient is not hypoxic. Current guidance is to titrate oxygen to the target range, not to give it reflexively.

options.text: Apply a nasal cannula at 2 L/min as a precaution
options.rationale: Oxygen is a drug; giving it without an indication is not a 'precaution,' and hyperoxia may cause harm in ACS.

options.text: Have the patient hyperventilate to increase oxygen
options.rationale: Hyperventilation does not meaningfully raise saturation in a patient already at 97% and can cause harm.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm current ACS oxygen guidance in AAOS 12e and AHA.

questions.stem: Which patient should receive high-concentration oxygen immediately, without waiting for a pulse oximetry reading?

options.text: A patient with a sprained ankle and normal breathing
options.rationale: No indication for oxygen.

options.text: A patient with signs of shock: pale, cool, clammy skin and a rapid weak pulse
options.rationale: Correct. Shock is a perfusion emergency; high-concentration oxygen is indicated regardless of the reading.

options.text: A patient with a mild headache and no other complaints
options.rationale: No indication for oxygen.

options.text: A patient who is anxious but has normal skin color and normal breathing
options.rationale: Anxiety alone is not an indication for oxygen; reassess and treat the cause.

questions.verify_notes: Confirm indications for high-concentration oxygen in AAOS 12e.
